paragraphs.heading: People power
paragraphs.text: Athenian democracy grew up around the 6th century BC in Athens, a Greek city-state, or polis, that took in the city itself and the surrounding land of Attica. Its name joins two Greek words, dêmos, people, and krátos, power, so it literally means people power. Only free adult men who were citizens could take part; women, minors and slaves could not. Those citizens were probably no more than 30 percent of all adults.

paragraphs.heading: Before democracy
paragraphs.text: Earlier, Athens was ruled by archons, or magistrates, and by the council of the Areopagus, made up of former archons, who were mostly aristocrats. In 621 BC Draco replaced laws passed on by word of mouth with a written code that only a court could enforce. Most of his laws were harsh and were later repealed. Still, putting law in writing was among the earliest efforts of this sort and is seen as an early step toward democracy.

paragraphs.heading: Solon's reforms
paragraphs.text: In 594 BC Solon was made chief archon and set out to ease the conflict caused by deep inequality. He gave every free resident of Attica a political role, including the right to attend the assembly, called the Ecclesia, which was open to all male citizens. He sorted citizens into four property classes by how much their estates produced each year. A council called the boule, with 400 members, ran daily business and set the agenda. He also cancelled existing debts, freed debtors, and banned borrowing with one's own person as security.

paragraphs.heading: Cleisthenes and the ten tribes
paragraphs.text: The young democracy was overthrown in 561 BC by the tyrant Peisistratos and restored after his son Hippias was expelled in 510. In 508 and 507 BC Cleisthenes weakened the leading aristocratic families and tied every Athenian to the running of the city. He made the old tribes politically meaningless and created ten new ones, built from small local units called demes, so that citizens were grouped by where they lived rather than by wealth. Each male citizen older than 18 had to be enrolled in his deme.

paragraphs.heading: Ephialtes and Pericles
paragraphs.text: A third round of reform came from Ephialtes in 462/1 BC. While his opponents were away helping the Spartans, he persuaded the assembly to cut the Areopagus down to a criminal court hearing homicide and sacrilege cases. Pericles was the longest-lasting democratic leader, guiding Athens from 461 to 429 BC. After his death, during the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta, oligarchic revolutions briefly halted the democracy twice, in 411 and 404 BC.

paragraphs.heading: Not the only democracy
paragraphs.text: Athens is the best-known Greek democracy, but it was neither the first nor the only one: several other city-states adopted similar constitutions before it, and Aristotle points to others. By the late 4th century BC, perhaps half of the more than a thousand Greek cities may have been democracies. Athens dominates the story because its record is fuller, including the only complete surviving constitution, which Aristotle and his students put together in the 4th century BCE.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word came from
paragraphs.text: By analogy with monarchy and oligarchy, you might expect the new system to be called demarchy. But that word was already in use and meant the office of a high town magistrate. The idea is first put into words around 470 BC in The Suppliants, in a line sung by the chorus. The word democracy then appears in Herodotus, who also uses isonomia, an older word for the same idea.
